questions.title: Java 21 Virtual Threads and Structured Concurrency
questions.question: What are virtual threads in Java 21, how do they differ from platform threads, and what is structured concurrency?

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Project Loom and how it changes the concurrency model for IO-bound Java services — a hot topic for any 2024+ backend role.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming virtual threads make CPU-bound code faster. They don't. Virtual threads only help when threads block on IO — they free the carrier thread to run other virtual threads during the block.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss pinning (synchronized blocks pin the carrier thread), thread-local variable caveats, and the StructuredTaskScope API for fan-out patterns with automatic cancellation.

questions.direct_answer: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads that mount on a small pool of OS (carrier) threads. When a virtual thread blocks on IO, it unmounts, freeing the carrier for another virtual thread. This enables a thread-per-request model at scale without the memory cost of millions of platform threads.

sections.title: Virtual Threads Make Thread-Per-Request Viable Again — But They Break ThreadLocal and synchronized Assumptions
sections.content:
Before virtual threads, Java's concurrency model had a fundamental tension: platform threads are **expensive** (~1MB stack, OS-scheduled, limited to thousands), so we pool and reuse them. But pooling introduces complexity — bounded queues, rejection policies, pool sizing, ThreadLocal cleanup.

**Virtual threads** (Java 21) resolve this by making threads **cheap**. A virtual thread's stack starts at ~1KB and grows as needed. The JVM schedules millions of virtual threads onto a small pool of **carrier threads** (platform threads managed by a ForkJoinPool). When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM **unmounts** it from the carrier — the carrier is immediately available for another virtual thread. No thread is wasted waiting.

This means **thread-per-request** is viable again. Instead of a pool of 200 threads handling 10,000 concurrent requests, create 10,000 virtual threads — one per request. Each virtual thread blocks naturally on I/O without wasting a platform thread.

The migration caveats are significant. **ThreadLocal** works but can leak memory because you might create millions of virtual threads. **synchronized blocks pin the virtual thread to the carrier** — the carrier cannot be reused while the virtual thread holds the monitor. Use `ReentrantLock` instead of `synchronized` to avoid pinning. And thread pool sizing becomes irrelevant — the JVM manages the carrier pool automatically.

sections.title: Carrier Pinning and the synchronized-to-ReentrantLock Migration
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Virtual threads: ~1KB stack, JVM-scheduled** — millions can run concurrently; carrier pool defaults to N = CPU cores.
- **Blocking I/O unmounts the virtual thread** — the carrier is freed for other work; thread-per-request scales to millions.
- **Carrier pinning** — `synchronized` block prevents unmounting; replace with `ReentrantLock` on I/O-heavy paths.
- **Do not pool virtual threads** — use `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`; pooling defeats the purpose.
- **`-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short`** — detects `synchronized` blocks that pin during testing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Virtual threads make thread-per-request viable by making threads cheap — ~1KB initial stack, JVM-scheduled onto a small pool of carrier threads.

**How they work:**
- When a virtual thread calls blocking I/O, it unmounts from the carrier — the carrier is freed for other virtual threads
- Millions can run concurrently; JVM manages scheduling; carrier pool defaults to N = number of CPU cores

**Carrier pinning (main migration concern):**
- `synchronized` block pins the virtual thread to its carrier — cannot unmount during the block
- If the block contains I/O, that carrier thread is wasted — effectively a blocking platform thread again
- Fix: replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` on I/O-heavy paths

**Migration guidelines:**
- Do not pool virtual threads — pooling defeats the purpose; use `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`
- `ThreadLocal` works but risks memory waste with millions of threads — ScopedValue is the replacement
- Enable `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short` during testing to find `synchronized` blocks that need migration

I recommend virtual threads for I/O-heavy workloads like HTTP servers and database-heavy services. CPU-bound computation still benefits from platform threads with ForkJoinPool.

beats.text: Before virtual threads, Java's concurrency model had a fundamental tension: platform threads are expensive (~1MB stack, OS-scheduled, limited to thousands), so we pool and reuse them. But pooling introduces complexity — bounded queues, rejection policies, pool sizing, ThreadLocal cleanup. Virtual threads (Java 21) resolve this by making threads cheap. A virtual thread's stack starts at ~1KB and grows as needed. The JVM schedules millions of virtual threads onto a small pool of carrier threads (platform threads managed by a ForkJoinPool). When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts.

steps: The biggest production concern with virtual threads is carrier pinning.
When a virtual thread enters a synchronized block and then blocks on I/O, the JVM cannot unmount it — the carrier thread is pinned and unavailable for other virtual threads.
This effectively turns the carrier pool into a traditional thread pool with the same concurrency limit.
If all carriers are pinned, the system has no threads available for new work — worse than a standard thread pool because the expectation was unlimited concurrency.

``java // PROBLEMATIC: synchronized pins the carrier synchronized (lock) { result = httpClient.send(request); // I/O blocks while pinned } // BETTER: ReentrantLock does not pin lock.lock(); try { result = httpClient.send(request); // I/O unmounts the virtual thread } finally { lock.unlock(); } ` The migration path: replace synchronized blocks that contain I/O with ReentrantLock.

items: Virtual threads: ~1KB stack, JVM-scheduled — millions can run concurrently; carrier pool defaults to N = CPU cores
Blocking I/O unmounts the virtual thread — the carrier is freed for other work; thread-per-request scales to millions
Carrier pinning — synchronized block prevents unmounting; replace with ReentrantLock on I/O-heavy paths
Do not pool virtual threads — use Executors
